problem_motivation.content: Pre-trained foundation MLIPs do not fully cover materials diversity and unseen conditions, so domain-specific calibration is needed

mechanism_principle.content: Equivariance is preserved because fixed CGCs enforce symmetry while learnable path weights only scale allowed interactions.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: These couplings, or symmetry-allowed interaction paths (Geiger & Smidt, 2022), are realized through Clebsch–Gordan coefficients (CGCs), which are predefined, non-trainable constants that mathematically guarantee equivariance.

mechanism_principle.content: Updating only the path-weight tensor preserves equivariance because symmetry is enforced by CGCs, not by the trainable weights.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Equivariance is strictly enforced by the predefined CGCs, while the capacity to learn lies entirely in the weights W. Therefore, when adapting a pre-trained model, the natural intervention point is this path-weight tensor. In other words, updating the path-weight tensor does not affect equivariance constraints.

mechanism_principle.content: Sparse fine-tuning keeps most path coefficients near zero, suppressing unnecessary degrees of freedom.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: To this end, we promote sparsity in ∆W by encouraging most path coefficients to remain close to zero, thereby suppressing unnecessary degrees of freedom during fine-tuning.

mechanism_principle.content: Symmetry is preserved during sparse adaptation because ΔW only modulates learnable weights on CGCs in tensor interaction paths.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Because ∆W modulates the learnable weights on CGCs in individual tensor interaction paths (see Appendix A), symmetry constraints are maintained, and equivariance is strictly preserved.

mechanism_principle.content: The instability of naive STR is attributed to coupled decay of threshold and weight updates.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: We empirically found that applying the naive STR causes instability during the fine-tuning process in equivariant MLIPs due to the coupled decay of τ and ∆W.

mechanism_principle.content: Linear parameters are inferred to be more important for preserving performance, so the model prunes them less readily.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This suggests that the linear parameters are more critical for maintaining performance and are thus pruned more reluctantly by the model

hypothesis_statement.content: The paper proposes a sparsity-promoting fine-tuning method that selectively updates parameters using structural properties of E(3)-equivariant models.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: To address this, we propose a sparsity-promoting fine-tuning method that selectively updates model parameters by exploiting the structural properties of E(3)-equivariant materials foundation models.

hypothesis_statement.content: Selective parameter updating can modify only target-domain-relevant parameters while keeping the rest intact
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: A complementary yet unexplored perspective is to instead control which parameters are updated, encouraging the model to selectively modify only those most relevant to the target domain while preserving the rest intact.

hypothesis_statement.content: The paper proposes a sparsity-promoting fine-tuning method for equivariant MLIPs that maintains equivariance via selective parameter updates
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: To bridge this gap, we propose a sparsity-promoting fine-tuning method for equivariant MLIPs, which carefully maintains equivariance with selective parameter updating.

hypothesis_statement.content: Selective updates of only critical interaction paths should yield more effective adaptation.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: We hypothesize that more effective adaptation can be achieved through selective updates, enabling the model to adaptively identify and modify only the most critical paths.

hypothesis_statement.content: The approach should generalize across diverse chemical domains rather than being limited to one material class.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span:
These results suggest that our approach is not confined to a single material class but
can generalize across diverse chemical domains, from inorganic crystals to organic molecules.

hypothesis_statement.content: The high-sparsity regime may compress adaptation into only the most essential parameter changes.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: We hypothesize that this high-sparsity regime forces the model to distill the adaptation into the most essential parameter updates.

hypothesis_statement.content: Extending non-magnetic foundation models is proposed as an efficient way to reuse pretrained knowledge while modeling magnetic energy differences.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Extending non-magnetic foundation models is therefore a highly efficient strategy, as it enables the reuse of pre-trained knowledge while capturing the subtle energy differences associated with magnetic configurations.

causal_claim.content: Fine-tuning reweights the relative contributions of interaction paths to adapt the model to target-domain characteristics such as composition or thermodynamic regime; in practice, injecting ΔW directly into the path-weight tensor enables this flexible domain adaptation with negligible computational overhead.
evidence_spans: From this perspective, fine-tuning corresponds to reweighting the relative contributions of interaction paths, thereby adjusting the model to the characteristics of the target dataset (e.g., composition, pressure/temperature regime, or the level of theory used in DFT calculations).
In practice, we inject ∆W directly into the path-weight tensor, introducing negligible computational overhead (see Section 5.5) while enabling flexible domain adaptation.

evidence_spans: In our case, only a subset of path weights corresponding to specific interaction paths is updated during adaptation, highlighting only the physically relevant interactions while suppressing symmetry-trivial paths.

mechanism_principle.content: The method is motivated by sparsity/Occam-style principles: physical phenomena are often governed by a few core variables, and reducing model complexity improves interpretability and generalization in scientific applications.
evidence_spans: based on the principle that physical phenomena are often governed by a few core variables
This reflects Occam’s razor, where reducing model complexity enhances both interpretability and generalization in scientific applications.

mechanism_principle.content: Equivariance is preserved during adaptation because symmetry is enforced by fixed, non-trainable Clebsch–Gordan coefficients (CGCs), while the trainable path weights or sparse updates (ΔW) only scale or modulate these symmetry-allowed interaction paths; therefore updating the path-weight tensor does not violate equivariance constraints.
evidence_spans: These couplings, or symmetry-allowed interaction paths (Geiger & Smidt, 2022), are realized through Clebsch–Gordan coefficients (CGCs), which are predefined, non-trainable constants that mathematically guarantee equivariance.

Equivariance is strictly enforced by the predefined CGCs, while the capacity to learn lies entirely in the weights W. Therefore, when adapting a pre-trained model, the natural intervention point is this path-weight tensor. In other words, updating the path-weight tensor does not affect equivariance constraints.
Because ∆W modulates the learnable weights on CGCs in individual tensor interaction paths (see Appendix A), symmetry constraints are maintained, and equivariance is strictly preserved.

mechanism_principle.content: Sparse fine-tuning works by keeping most path-coefficient updates near zero, suppressing unnecessary degrees of freedom during adaptation.
evidence_spans: To this end, we promote sparsity in ∆W by encouraging most path coefficients to remain close to zero, thereby suppressing unnecessary degrees of freedom during fine-tuning.

mechanism_principle.content: Naive STR becomes unstable during fine-tuning because the decay of the threshold τ is coupled to the updates/decay of ΔW.
evidence_spans: We empirically found that applying the naive STR causes instability during the fine-tuning process in equivariant MLIPs due to the coupled decay of τ and ∆W.

mechanism_principle.content: Linear parameters appear more critical for preserving model performance, so the pruning mechanism removes them more reluctantly.
evidence_spans: This suggests that the linear parameters are more critical for maintaining performance and are thus pruned more reluctantly by the model

hypothesis_statement.content: The paper hypothesizes that sparsity-promoting fine-tuning for E(3)-equivariant MLIPs/materials foundation models—by selectively updating only target-domain-relevant or critical interaction-path parameters while preserving the rest and maintaining equivariance—will enable more effective adaptation.
evidence_spans: To address this, we propose a sparsity-promoting fine-tuning method that selectively updates model parameters by exploiting the structural properties of E(3)-equivariant materials foundation models.

A complementary yet unexplored perspective is to instead control which parameters are updated, encouraging the model to selectively modify only those most relevant to the target domain while preserving the rest intact.
To bridge this gap, we propose a sparsity-promoting fine-tuning method for equivariant MLIPs, which carefully maintains equivariance with selective parameter updating.
We hypothesize that more effective adaptation can be achieved through selective updates, enabling the model to adaptively identify and modify only the most critical paths.

hypothesis_statement.content: The paper hypothesizes that a high-sparsity regime compresses adaptation into only the most essential parameter changes.
evidence_spans: We hypothesize that this high-sparsity regime forces the model to distill the adaptation into the most essential parameter updates.

hypothesis_statement.content: The approach is expected to generalize across diverse chemical domains rather than being limited to a single material class.
evidence_spans: These results suggest that our approach is not confined to a single material class but can generalize across diverse chemical domains, from inorganic crystals to organic molecules.

hypothesis_statement.content: Extending non-magnetic foundation models is proposed as an efficient way to reuse pretrained knowledge while modeling magnetic energy differences.
evidence_spans: Extending non-magnetic foundation models is therefore a highly efficient strategy, as it enables the reuse of pre-trained knowledge while capturing the subtle energy differences associated with magnetic configurations.

evidence_result.content: Across molecular, crystalline, and magnetic benchmarks, the method matches or exceeds full fine-tuning and ELoRA while updating only a small fraction of parameters—typically under 3% and in some cases as little as 0.5%—and this generalizes across equivariant architectures including MACE and NequIP-OAM-L.
evidence_spans: On energy and force prediction tasks across molecular and crystalline benchmarks, our method matches or surpasses full fine-tuning and equivariant low-rank adaptation while updating only ∼3 % of parameters, and in some cases as little as ∼0.5 %.

Applied to MACE potentials (Batatia et al., 2022; 2025; Kov´acs et al., 2025) across molecular, crystalline, and magnetic benchmarks, our method matches or exceeds the accuracy of full fine-tuning while updating only 0.5-3 % of parameters.

In this section, we present experimental results demonstrating that our method is comparable to or superior to baselines such as full fine-tuning and ELoRA across all domains. Remarkably, these gains are achieved by modifying fewer than 3 % of the total parameters, with some tasks requiring updates to as few as 0.5 %.

As shown in Table I in Appendix D, our method achieves comparable or superior accuracy to full fine-tuning and ELoRA across all bench- mark datasets, demonstrating its generalizability across different equivariant architectures.

evidence_result.content: The method generalizes beyond energy/force recalibration to additional material properties, including magnetic moment prediction and magnetism-aware total energy modeling.
evidence_spans: Beyond energy and force calibration, we further demonstrate task generalizability by applying our method to magnetic moment prediction and magnetism-aware total energy modeling.
Beyond recalibrating energy and force predictions, it extends effectively to other material properties such as magnetic moments, demonstrating broader applicability of foundation MLIPs.

Finally, analysis of sparsity patterns reveals which coefficients are selectively updated, yielding physical insights into the learned representations.

evidence_result.content: On rMD17, the low-sparsity setup surpasses both full fine-tuning and ELoRA on eight of ten molecules, while the high-sparsity setup still outperforms ELoRA across all molecules.

Even more impressively, our method in a high-sparsity setup (H) also outperforms ELoRA across all molecules, showing the robustness of our sparse adaptation strategy on diverse organic systems.

evidence_result.content: As λτ increases, Linear-only sparsity grows gradually whereas All sparsity rises sharply earlier; the energy plots reveal two effective adaptation regimes: a low-sparsity, high-performance regime and a high-sparsity, stable regime. For most datasets the best compact-update point in the low-sparsity regime is at λτ = 0.01, except TM-O-Spin where it is 0.05; a high-sparsity stable regime emerges from λτ ≈ 0.3 and retains strong performance despite extreme sparsity.
evidence_spans: As shown in Figure 1, for the Linear-only strategy, sparsity increases gradually with increasing λτ. In contrast, for the All strategy, module sparsity increases sharply at a much earlier stage.
Furthermore, the energy plots for both the Linear and All settings commonly exhibit two distinct, effective adaptation regimes.
This corresponds to λτ = 0.01 for most datasets, except for the TM-O-Spin, where the optimum occurs at λτ = 0.05.
Second, we identified a high-sparsity, stable regime (labeled as Ours (H)) at larger λτ from 0.3, which maintains strong performance with extreme sparsity despite being slightly sub-optimal.

constraint.content: Fine-tuning equivariant GNNs must preserve equivariance constraints—specifically translational, rotational, and reflectional symmetries in 3D space.
